claims.text: The initial catalyst consists of approximately 16.4–16.8 nm FCC Pd nanocubes with {100} facets and an approximately 1.0 nm, equiatomic PtRuFeCoNi shell.
The as-synthesized PtRuFeCoNi shell is randomly mixed, disordered, and metastable.
The catalyst's high ethanol-oxidation performance is governed by its disordered multielement {100} shell.
Cocktail effects, local lattice distortion, and orbital hybridization in the disordered shell produce a broad or continuous distribution of adsorption sites.
The adsorption sites in the disordered shell bind ethanol-oxidation intermediates at near-optimal strengths.
Relevant intermediates whose adsorption is tuned include adsorbed CO, acetaldehyde, and acetate.
Balanced intermediate adsorption prevents surface poisoning while enabling efficient C–C bond cleavage and complete 12-electron ethanol oxidation.
Electron transfer among the constituent metals facilitates bond cleavage.
Controlled thermal annealing can induce local L10 or L12 atomic ordering in the PtRuFeCoNi shell.
Atomic ordering limits active-site diversity and perturbs beneficial orbital overlap in the shell.
An annealed, ordered catalyst will have lower ethanol-oxidation current density than the as-synthesized disordered catalyst.
An annealed, ordered catalyst will exhibit a higher onset potential or overpotential than the disordered catalyst.
An annealed, ordered catalyst will have lower durability because of more pronounced surface poisoning.
The as-synthesized disordered Pd@PtRuFeCoNi nanocubes exhibit high ethanol-oxidation efficiency and durability.
The proposed mechanism should apply under acidic ethanol-electrooxidation conditions at temperatures below 80°C.
At substantially higher temperatures or very different electrolyte pH, alternative reaction pathways or catalyst reconstruction may dominate.
